content.content:
The cold read's fixes to the landed rules

After the thirteen items landed, a worker given only the coordinator skill read the parts that they changed. This is a cold read. It flagged 27 passages that could send its reader wrong or make it search: 12 in SKILL.md, 2 in batch.md, 6 in delegating.md, 3 in record.md and 4 in sources.md. The skill writer fixed all 27 on the branch skill/coordinator-cold-read-fixes, in one commit. The fixes change the wording, not the rules. None of them is on main.

This section shows the 20 fixes that answer the 23 flags of the four parts that the coordinator reads for its work. It leaves out sources.md, the file that names each rule's source, since no worker reads it for a task. Each fix names the landed rule that it touches, then shows the old text collapsed and the new text whole, with the added words underlined. The reasons sit below each part's fixes, outside the Select button's range.

References
  • The cold read's report of 1 November, which gives each flag with its problem, its confidence and a proposed fix; the skill writer's report of 1 November; commit 10532a220 on the branch skill/coordinator-cold-read-fixes, and its diff against main.

Part 1 of 4 · 11 fixes for 12 flagsSKILL.md, the main file

  1. Rule 1, Keep the context for decisions. “The standing goal”, the second bullet, its last sentence.

    Old text (tap to open)

    Read a worker's final message yourself.

    New text

    Read each worker's final message yourself, and brief the worker to keep that message a summary.

  2. Rule 7, The boot loads the parts that the work needs. “The standing goal”, a new third bullet. Its sentence moves here from step 7 of “The boot”.

    Old text (tap to open)

    Step 7 of “The boot”, its second sentence

    Load references/delegating.md before any reading that a worker could do.

    New text
    • Give a worker any reading beyond the boot's steps that a worker could do. Load references/delegating.md first.

  3. Rule 3, No labels from the coordinator's reasoning. “Talking to the curator”, the third bullet, its first two sentences.

    Old text (tap to open)

    Use no internal shorthand, and no label from your own reasoning that the curator has not seen. The curator knows the terms that the skills define.

    New text

    Use no internal shorthand, and no label that you coined, unless you defined it to the curator earlier in this conversation. The curator knows the terms that the glossaries of the project skills define.

  4. Rule 5, Questions in chat, rewrites as a diff. “Pages”, the first bullet, its second sentence.

    Old text (tap to open)

    Put a question to the curator in chat, not on a page.

    New text

    Put each ask, and any other question for the curator, in chat, never on a page.

  5. Rule 5, Questions in chat, rewrites as a diff. “Pages”, the second bullet.

    Old text (tap to open)

    On the page, show each rewritten entry or section as a diff: its current text collapsed, then the change. Below it, say what the change alters in the work, outside the Select button's range.

    New text

    On the page, show each rewritten entry or section as a diff. Show its current text collapsed, then its new text whole, with the cut and added words marked. Below it, say what the change alters in the work, outside the range of every Select button.

  6. Rule 6, A Select button for each entry. “Pages”, the third bullet, from its second sentence.

    Old text (tap to open)

    So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading and beside each entry of a part, which selects that section's text for Speak. A part's button selects the whole part.

    New text

    So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, and beside each item of a section. A section's button selects the whole section for Speak, its items included. An item's button selects that item.

  7. Rule 7, The boot loads the parts that the work needs. “The record: what goes where”, the bullet on the boot note, the end of its first sentence.

    Old text (tap to open)

    the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages.

    New text

    the armed check-ins, by name; the URLs of live pages; and the parts of the skills that the work in hand needs.

  8. Rule 7, The boot loads the parts that the work needs. “The boot”, step 7.

    Old text (tap to open)

    7. Load the parts of the skills that the work in hand needs, as the boot note names them. Load references/delegating.md before any reading that a worker could do.

    New text

    7. Load the parts of the skills that the work in hand needs: those that the boot note names, and for other work, those that “The parts” names.

  9. Rule 8, A calibration check after a compaction. “The boot”, step 8.

    Old text (tap to open)

    8. After a compaction, if the curator is not away (“Quiet times”), give a calibration check in a few short lines: the project's history, the current goals, where the work stands, and the next moves. Leave out a running batch.

    New text

    8. After a compaction, if the curator is not away (“Quiet times”), give the curator a calibration check. In a few short lines, state your picture of the project's history, the current goals, where the work stands and the next moves. The curator corrects it. This check may restate what POSITIONS holds. Leave out a running batch. Then go on with the work that may start.

  10. Rules 7 and 8. “A light boot”, a new second sentence.

    Old text (tap to open)

    When the curator asks for a light boot, take steps 0 and 3 to 8, and skip steps 1 and 2: FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX stay unread.

    New text

    When the curator asks for a light boot, take steps 0 and 3 to 8, and skip steps 1 and 2: FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX stay unread. For step 8, read POSITIONS' history with facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md#History he knows'.

  11. Rule 7, The boot loads the parts that the work needs. “The parts”, the line on delegating.md.

    Old text (tap to open)

    references/delegating.md: before you brief, launch, watch or resume any worker.

    New text

    references/delegating.md: before you brief, launch, watch or resume any worker, and before any reading that a worker could do.

Why each fix, by its number:

  1. When a worker's final message is itself a long report, the old sentence did not say whether to read it or give it to a worker to condense.
  2. In step 7, the sentence could read as a boot step or as a standing rule, and as “load the part, then read” or “load the part, then give the reading away”.
  3. After a compaction, the coordinator cannot know which labels you saw, so it could not follow the old text. The old text also did not say which skills' terms count.
  4. “Question” is not the skill's defined word “ask”, so the old sentence left unclear which questions it covers.
  5. “The change” could mean the new text whole or a line-by-line diff, and Speak reads a line-by-line diff badly. With a button for each section and each item, a note outside an item's range could still be inside its section's range. The new text follows your words of 21:45 on 28 October: “as diffs, like before, with original collapsed, reasons below (outside selection range)”.
  6. In the skill, “part” means a file under references/ and “entry” a line of FACTS or POSITIONS, and the old text used both words for pieces of a page.
  7. Step 7 loads the parts that the boot note names, but the boot note's list of contents did not include them.
  8. With no parts named in the boot note, the old step read as “load nothing”. Its second sentence moved to “The standing goal”, fix 2.
  9. The old step clashed with two rules: do not restate what POSITIONS says, and do not explain again the history that you know. It also did not say whether to wait for your correction or go on with the work.
  10. In a light boot, POSITIONS stays unread, and the old text did not say how to print the history that step 8 needs. The writer checked that the command and the heading exist.
  11. “The parts” did not list this occasion to load delegating.md.
References
  • The cold read's flags, by fix: 1, S1; 2, S9; 3, S2 and S3; 4, S4; 5, S5 and S6; 6, S7; 7, S8; 8, S8 and S9; 9, S10 and S11; 10, S12; 11, S9.
  • Fix 5: explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-10-28/evidence/briefing-practice.md, section 17, as the skill writer's report cites it.
  • SKILL.md on main and on the branch.

Part 2 of 4 · 2 fixes for 2 flagsbatch.md, the part on batches

  1. Proposal 1, The distance in every batch until the switch-over. “The checker count and the distance”, the first sentence.

    Old text (tap to open)

    The gate reports the checker count and the distance in every batch until the switch-over.

    New text

    Until the switch-over lands, the gate of every batch reports the checker count and the distance.

  2. Proposal 3, Push main only from the main tree. “While it runs”, the second bullet, its last two sentences.

    Old text (tap to open)

    Push main from no tree but the main tree. A push from another tree makes git refuse the landing's push, which the commit stage makes on top of the main tree's head.

    New text

    Keep origin/main at or behind the main tree's head, or git refuses the commit stage's push. So push main from no other tree. From the main tree, push nothing that the batch committed: the commit stage pushes it.

Why each fix, by its number:

  1. The old sentence could read as a fact about the batch script or as an order, and “until the switch-over” as until it starts or until it ends. The script's gate runs both counts in every batch.
  2. The old rule read both as a standing rule and as a rule for the run. A push from the main tree during a run could send the batch's commits before the commit stage does, or send a push that is to wait for you.
References
  • The cold read's flags, by fix: 1, B1; 2, B2.
  • batch.md on main and on the branch.

1. Rule 9, Sonnet fetches words, Opus writes reports. “Which tier runs what”, the second bullet.

    Old text (tap to open)

    Use Sonnet for archaeology and retrieval of exact words only, never for a judgement or a summary. Have an Opus worker turn the evidence into a report, and condense a large report into a summary or the exact quotes that you need. Run it at extra high effort for a large report.

    New text

    Use Sonnet only for archaeology and to fetch exact words from a place that you name, never for a judgement or a summary. Have an Opus worker turn the evidence into a report, and choose from a long report the summary or the quotes that a question needs.

  2. Rule 9, Sonnet fetches words, Opus writes reports. “Which tier runs what”, a new third bullet, from the last sentence of the bullet before it.

    Old text (tap to open)

    Run it at extra high effort for a large report.

    New text
    • Run an Opus worker that writes or condenses a long report at extra high effort, xhigh. The Agent tool takes it as its effort option, and agent() as opts.effort. A headless session keeps its default effort unless its command sets one.

  3. Rule 10, Fable writes no permanent text. “Which tier runs what”, the bullet on writers.

    Old text (tap to open)

    Run every writer on Opus: of skill text, of record entries, and of each longer report or page for the curator, also when this session runs on Fable. Fable writes no text that goes as written into the permanent record, since its compressed register degrades the reasoning. It may give its reasoning as corrections to a text that Opus writes, and its review may edit a batch record in place. This holds while Fable is at 5.1.

    New text

    Run every writer on Opus: of skill text, of record entries, and of each longer report or page for the curator, also when this session runs on Fable. No Fable worker writes such text, since its compressed register degrades the reasoning. A Fable worker may comment on a text that Opus writes, and Opus words each correction into the text. A Fable review may edit a batch record in place. On Fable, this session still writes its own state: the boot note, the held list, PLAN's lines, the review queue and commit messages.

  4. Rule 10, Fable writes no permanent text. “Which tier runs what”, a new fourth bullet, from the last sentence of the bullet before it.

    Old text (tap to open)

    This holds while Fable is at 5.1.

    New text
    • The rules on Fable's text hold while Fable is at version 5.1. When this session runs on Fable, explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh prints its version.

  5. Proposal 2, No stash after a killed gather. “Interrupts and process stops”, the bullet on a killed gather.

    Old text (tap to open)

    If a batch's gather was killed mid-work, resume the run with the main tree as the gather left it. The gather's recovery prompt takes the uncommitted changes as its earlier attempt's work.

    New text

    If a batch's gather was killed mid-work, resume the run, and leave the main tree as the gather left it. On the resume, the batch script's recoverGather() gives the gather a prompt that takes the uncommitted changes as its earlier attempt's work. You write no prompt. The check for a clean tree is the gather's first start's only.

Why each fix, by its number:

  1. The bullet gave both Sonnet and Opus the work of taking exact words, so the coordinator could not tell which tier takes quotes from a long report. “Large report” is now “long report”, here and in SKILL.md, so that one word names one thing.
  2. The part said how to name a worker's tier, but not how to set its effort, and “it” and “large” were unclear. Neither script that starts a headless session passes an effort setting, so the bullet names none.
  3. “Permanent record” is not the skill's defined word “record”, and the old text left unclear whether the rule binds this session when it runs on Fable. If Fable's corrections went in word for word, Fable's text would go into the record as written. The new text follows your words of 07:12 and 07:47 on 27 October.
  4. The old sentence did not say how to read Fable's version, or which sentences “this” covers. The script reads only this session's model, not what a worker on Fable runs.
  5. The coordinator could not tell whether it must write the gather's prompt, as it does for the commit stage. A resume on a tree with changes also seemed to break the gather's check for a clean tree. The writer checked recoverGather() and the gather's start in the batch script.

Part 4 of 4 · 2 fixes for 3 flagsrecord.md, the part on the record

  1. Rule 14, A position holds your meaning. “What an entry is”, the third bullet.

    Old text (tap to open)

    A POSITIONS entry holds the curator's meaning, not the curator's voice, factually correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it compounds.

    New text

    A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's words, not the curator's own words, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions. If the curator's words rest on a fact that is wrong, bring it to the curator by one of the three ways (SKILL.md, “The curator's role and decisions”). Correct the entry only after that.

  2. Rule 16, No general rule as an entry's reason. “What an entry is”, the fourth bullet.

    Old text (tap to open)

    An entry gives no general rule that holds for every decision, such as P-26, as its reason.

    New text

    Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).

  1. “Factually correct” could read as “fix a wrong fact in the curator's words, silently”, which would bend your decision. “Compounds” and “voice” are figures of speech.
  2. The reader had to look up the entry by its number to learn what kind of rule was meant, and the bullet did not say what reason to give instead.

File of a skill, such as delegating.md in its references/ folder; on this page, its main file SKILL.md too.
router
List in a skill's main file that names which part to load for which work; in fortress-repo, its section “The parts”.
transcript
File that holds a session's messages and tool calls.
draft
Text of a rule on the branch skill/coordinator-held-rules, as version 3 of this page showed it.
regrounded rule
Rule written again from your words at the time that you stated it.
land
Recommendation to put a new text into a skill on main.
fold
Recommendation to put a point into a sentence that a skill already has.
drop
Recommendation to leave a draft out of the skills.
proposal
Rule that the coordinator drafted, not from your words.
trailer
Closing lines of a commit message, which name who wrote the commit and in which session.
cold read
Reading of a skill by a worker given only the skill, which flags each passage that would send its reader wrong or make it search.
flag
Passage that a cold read marks, with its problem and a proposed fix.
fix
Skill writer's change of one passage, which answers one flag or two.
thread
Comment on a page, with its replies.
turn
Coordinator's work in answer to one message or comment.
harness
Program that runs the session and its tools, Claude Code.
scout
Sonnet worker that fetches exact words from the transcripts or git.
librarian
Opus worker that reads what a scout gathered and writes a summary.
headless session
Session that the coordinator starts from the shell with claude -p.
Agent tool
Tool that launches a worker inside the coordinating session.
workflow
Script that the Workflow tool runs, with one agent for each step.
agent()
Call in a workflow script that launches one agent.
effort
Setting of how much a model reasons before it answers, from low to max; extra high is xhigh.
SendMessage
Tool that sends a message to a worker.
facts-extract.sh
Script that prints a record entry by its number, and its history on request.
model-now.sh
Script that prints the model of this session's turn.
INDEX
Record of one line for each note under explorations/.
boot note
File of what is in flight now, explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md.
PLAN
Working plan of the project, explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md.
review queue
File of the items that wait for your word or your review.
light boot
Shorter boot that you can ask for, which leaves FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX unread.
calibration check
Few lines after a compaction in which the coordinator states its picture of the project, for you to correct.
pass
Coordinator's rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the record's form.
consolidation
Pass over whole sections of the record at once.
clarity workflow
Workflow that rewrites FACTS or POSITIONS entries so that each reads on its own.
gather
Stage of a batch that merges the work of its tasks into the main tree.
recoverGather()
Function of the batch script that gives a killed gather its prompt on a resume.
commit stage
Last stage of a batch, which commits the landed tree, runs the pass and pushes the tree.
gate
Full check of a tree before it lands.
checker count
Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.
distance
All the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library, which must reach zero before the switch-over.
switch-over
Move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library.
three principles
Team's later word, the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do, which settle most design questions.
team's later word
Positions that the team's type group reached after the specification's early text, which win where the two conflict.
consequential decision
Decision that reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of yours, touches microGPT, chooses among ways that the record and the three principles do not settle, or cannot be undone.
three ways
Ways in which a consequential decision reaches you: asked before the work, landed and then reviewed, or held for your answer.
ask
Message that puts one decision to you.
fork
Design question with more than one way forward.
peers
Other programming languages whose ways the coordinator compares, such as Swift.
provenance
Origin of a text: who wrote it, in which role, when, and whether it was reviewed.
open-source years
Years after the team made Fortress open source, when people outside the team could contribute.

An Opus worker made this page on 30 October 2026 and updated it on 31 October, at the coordinator's brief. Another Opus worker made version 4 on 2 November. Version 4 draws on the note skill-rules-regrounded-2026-11-01.md, the branch skill/coordinator-cold-read-fixes, the cold read's report and the skill writer's report of 1 November, and the held list. It changes no file in the repository.

# Keeping the record

How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.

**history**
: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.

**pointer**
: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."

**pass**
: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- A POSITIONS entry holds the curator's meaning, not the curator's voice, factually correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it compounds.
- An entry gives no general rule that holds for every decision, such as P-26, as its reason.
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## A consolidation

A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. Run it on FACTS before each batch launches, since the batch's workers read it.

- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.

## The consolidation tools

Three Workflow scripts make the record and the worker skill readable again when they drift. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Put the open questions of their runs on the review queue.

- The mining workflow finds where each POSITIONS entry came from: the curator's words, or an agent's summary or default. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
- The clarity workflow rewrites POSITIONS or FACTS entries so that each reads on its own. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is" (scope, present meaning, evidence, comprehension, ownership and consistency), and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Run it when entries no longer read on their own. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
- The orientation workflow writes `fortress-repo`'s revival part, the short account of how revived Fortress differs from the original, which every worker reads whole. Its consolidate mode rewrites the whole part. Run it when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Its update mode runs after each landing (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"). Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`.

## INDEX and the gap ledger

- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
- Put a run's working files in an `evidence/` folder beside its results file: its briefs, chunks and checks, and the worker reports that the results draw on. Move them there with `git mv` once the results are judged. Only the results file gets an INDEX line. `check-index.sh` skips evidence folders. Do not add a folder's name to its list to let the folder pass.
- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.
- Ask the curator before you regroup the ledger's rows or derive its views again.

<!-- The record-landing workflow: after a climb batch's post-batch review, bring the record in line with the landing (FACTS, POSITIONS and their histories, the ledger rows the evidence names, PLAN, PLAN-history, the review queue, INDEX and line fixes in other notes) in a worktree of its own, and hand the coordinator one diff; how to launch it, what it writes, and how the coordinator lands its branch. -->

# The record-landing workflow

`record-landing.js` does the record's work after a landing, which the coordinator did by hand through a record writer and a routing worker until climb batch 24. It is the smallest first version of the design `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-landing-workflow.md` (`5384a4f35`), which the curator approved with its eight defaults on 2026-11-02. It runs in five stages, in the pattern of the orientation workflow (`../orientation/orientation.js`):

1. **Sort** (Opus, `sort.md`): `prepare.sh` makes the worktree and its branch and writes the evidence into the run's folder (`evidence.py`'s header lists its six files; `plan.md` ends with the PLAN lines that look stale, from `plan-moves.py --stale-at`); the sorter reads it, the review's routing part and the batch record's items, and writes `owed.md`, one line per change with its number, its home, its kind, its weight, its ground and its writer, and marks each kind and each "Needed by" that no source states as set by the workflow.
2. **Write**: a Sonnet driver runs `drive.sh 1` in the background and waits for it in steps of 240 s, under the five minutes that its prompt cache lives. `drive.sh` starts two headless Opus writer streams side by side through the worktree's copy of `../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`: the entries writer (`entries.md`: FACTS, POSITIONS, an entry's history, ledger rows, as `record.apply` and `rows.rewrite`) and the routing writer (`routing.md`: PLAN, PLAN-history, the queue, INDEX, other notes, edited in the worktree). Then `checks.sh 1` writes `mech-1.md`.
3. **Check**: the checker (`check.md`: coverage, fidelity, form and routing) and the clarity cold reader (`../record-clarity/coldread.md`, unchanged, told to write its report in parts of five entries) on `clean.txt`, side by side.
4. **Fix**: `drive.sh 2` resumes both streams once with the three reports, then `checks.sh 2` writes `mech-2.md`.
5. **Judge** (Opus, `judge.md`): apply or hold each change once, `final.apply` and `final.rewrite`, `diff.md` (within 10,000 characters), and `final.sh`, which runs every check again and makes two commits on the branch. The judge writes nothing after the commits.

The mechanical checks (`checks.sh`): the six record files reset to the worktree's base, the cut-only POSITIONS lines checked with `../record-clarity/words-subset.py --root`, the writers' files applied with `record.py apply` and `../ledger-clarity/apply.py`, each history block "by climb batch N landing workflow (Opus)"; then `record.py check --base`, `ledger.py check`, `ledger.py landing-check`, `check-index.sh`, `plan-moves.py`, `queue-check.py` and `lengths.py`.

- `plan-moves.py` fails a line out of PLAN that is not word for word in PLAN-history. Its `LOOK` lines, which never fail, name each PLAN line that still looks stale: a line whose own review-queue item is in (a), a list of items that names a settled one or differs from the queue's list that it names, and a review finding that a commit outside the record names. The checker takes each as a coverage failure, unless `owed.md` or the routing report says why the line stays.
- `queue-check.py` fails a gap in the new numbers, a new open item without "Needed by", a count that its items do not make, and an item new in "Answered by a decision of his" that cites no word of his on that same item, or that names a default taken without him ("at its default", "by the coordinator"). Such an item stays open, landed and then reviewed. The rule leans to keeping an item open: a true answer of his worded with those phrases fails too, and is reworded.
- `lengths.py` informs: each changed entry's length, and each entry already over 600 that grew, which the judge holds unless the owed clause alone explains the growth.

`drive.sh --dry-run` prints the commands of a round and starts nothing. The streams' headless sessions run `facts-extract.sh` and the `git` reads that `writer-stream.sh` allows, and not `record.py`, `ledger.py` or the checks, which need an approval that a headless session cannot get. So `checks.sh` is the first to apply and check the writers' files, after each round, and the fix round reads its output in `mech-1.md`.

Every brief reads the record only through `facts-extract.sh`, `record.py` and `ledger.py` in the worktree, and entries are written only through `record.py`. The run takes three arguments and no text, so a run gives the workflow data, never rules of its own. The briefs change only at the curator's yes.

## Running it

After the post-batch review is committed:

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/record-landing.js',
               args: { batch: 'N', base: 'BASE', landing: 'LANDING' } })

It makes `/home/user/fortress-landing-N` on the branch `record/landing-N` at `main`'s head. A replay adds `at`, the commit to make the worktree at, and its worktree and branch end in `-replay`. The replay of climb batch 24's landing, before the first live run at climb batch 25's:

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/record-landing.js',
               args: { batch: '24', base: 'b0f6cd6b7', landing: '25238e60c', at: '43cd61b62' } })

That one runs in `/home/user/fortress-landing-24-replay` on `record/landing-24-replay`. A killed run resumes with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte; each script skips a step whose output exists. During a run the coordinator writes none of the files that the workflow writes; a decision that the curator gives meanwhile is recorded after the landing. The design's estimate for a landing like climb batch 24's was 0.9M to 1.7M tokens written and 1 to 1.5 hours; the replay wrote 2.06M in 65 minutes (`process-engineering/record-landing-replay-24.md`, section 6). With the driver's waits under five minutes and the cold read in parts, a like landing writes about 1.8M, an estimate.

## What it writes

Everything goes in the worktree; the main tree is not touched. The run's folder, `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/record-landing/` in the worktree, holds `run.env`, the evidence, `owed.md`, the writers' files, briefs and reports, `check.md`, `cold-read.md`, `mech-1.md`, `mech-2.md`, `mech-final.md`, `final.apply`, `final.rewrite`, the commit messages and `diff.md`, and the logs of the rounds, which git ignores. The markers of finished rounds are in the worktree's `tmp/record-landing/`, which git ignores too, so the worktree is clean after the commits. The branch holds two commits: FACTS, POSITIONS, their histories and the ledger; then PLAN, PLAN-history, the queue, INDEX, the other notes and the run's folder. Each message ends "By the climb batch N landing workflow (Opus).", then the committing part's footer. The workflow's result names the worktree, the branch and `diff.md`; the judge's final message gives the two hashes.

## Landing its result

The coordinator reads `diff.md`, the judge's final message and `git -C WORKTREE show --stat` of the two commits, not the record. Then, on `main`:

1. `git cherry-pick` the two commits of the branch, in order.
2. `record.py check --base <main before the picks>` and `ledger.py landing-check <the batch's base>`.
3. Push, in the order of the `fortress-repo` skill's committing part.
4. `git worktree remove` the worktree, and delete the branch.

On a conflict, it applies `final.apply` with `record.py apply` on `main`, and cherry-picks the routing commit alone. The landing report names each POSITIONS change with its old and its new words, from `diff.md`, by the curator's rule of 2026-10-31. Each held change: run it again, file it in the queue, or leave it. Each "Needed by" and each kind that the workflow set, and each move to (a)'s "Answered by a decision of his", are in `diff.md`'s "For the curator", and wait for the coordinator to confirm. "Next" in `diff.md` gives the orientation update's call, run after the landing. The replay lands nothing on `main`: an Opus worker compares its two commits with the hand-made ones (`be3b07aac`, `08cc69e2d`, `b49631cb4`, `85b2998e9`), change by change.

<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

# Running and reviewing a batch

The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.

**batch record**
: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.

**base**
: Commit that the batch starts from.

**gather**
: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.

**merged-diff review**
: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.

**repair round**
: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.

**commit stage**
: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.

**reserved point**
: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.

**checker count**
: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.

**distance**
: All the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library, which must reach zero before the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library. The gate's distance stage counts them (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`), and FACTS holds the current value.

## The go

- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

## The checker count and the distance

The gate reports the checker count and the distance in every batch until the switch-over. Neither turns the gate red.

- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.

## Reserved points and repairs

- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.

## While it runs

- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
- From the launch until the run ends, by landing, by stopping or by holding its push for the curator, edit no tracked file in the main tree, the boot note included. The gather needs `git status --porcelain` there to print nothing. Push `main` from no tree but the main tree. A push from another tree makes git refuse the landing's push, which the commit stage makes on top of the main tree's head.
- Before the launch, name the check-in file in the boot note: `<scratchpad>/batch<N>/checkins.txt`, where `<N>` is the batch's number. After the launch, write the run's ID and each armed check-in's ID in that file. If the scratchpad loses a check-in's ID, find the check-in again with `list_triggers`.
- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.

## The landing

The landing check is `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, run by the gather and by the merged-diff review on the batch's base. It reports a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test removed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status. A finding the base already had counts too. The gather clears each finding before its commit, through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or by a reworded entry. The merged-diff review clears any that is left in its corrections commit. So a batch lands only when the check prints nothing.

If the batch's push is held for the curator, take the steps below at once on the local commits. Only the push waits, and the parts of the routing that need the pushed hashes.

1. Sweep the batch agents' to-dos from the session's shared task list: `explorations/coordinator/tools/sweep-tasks.py --delete`. If another workflow still runs, add `--running`, which removes only the completed tasks. The agents write these to-dos themselves, and the harness shows the whole list to every agent.
2. Check that the commit stage folded the batch's entries into FACTS (`references/record.md`, "The pass").
3. Run the orientation workflow in update mode on the landing's new and changed FACTS and POSITIONS entries, since the revival part cites decisions in most rules. `git diff <base> -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md` lists them. The workflow writes new text for each section of `fortress-repo`'s `revival-changes.md` that they touch. Have the writer install the sections that its judge accepts (`references/skill-rewrite.md`).
4. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
5. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing").
6. File what the review finds in PLAN. Then make these moves yourself. The manual's section "After the landing: the coordinator's routing" gives `PLAN-history.md`'s heading for each landing and the form of the one line.
   - Move word for word into `PLAN-history.md` each item that the batch built, each question that the batch or the curator answered, and each stale item. A stale item is one that a decision or a landed change has made moot.
   - If another home holds an open item's whole text, cut it in PLAN to one line with a pointer there. If it holds part, first move the rest there. This holds for the review lists too: an entry that `review-queue.md` holds becomes such a line.
   - Repoint each citation of a moved item: `git grep -n 'PLAN\.md' -- explorations/coordinator/*.md explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md .claude/skills`.
